CHAPTER 4.1 · LEARNING AREA 4 · NOVEMBER

Population and sample

Nobody asks all voters before making a forecast. Nobody opens every packet to check the filling quantity. You take a sample and draw conclusions from it about the whole. How well that works depends on how the sample is drawn and how large it is. This is where inferential statistics begins: estimating and testing with probabilities.

4 LESSONS2 UNITSFROM THE SAMPLE TO THE WHOLE
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • tell population and sample apart and check samples for representativeness
  • distinguish estimation problems and testing problems in examples
  • calculate the sample mean and the sample variance
  • understand how much sample results vary and how the sample size changes that

UNIT 12 LESSONS

1Population, sample, estimating and testing

In a survey of 1,000 randomly selected voters, 420 say they will vote for party X. What percentage is it in the whole population?

The best estimate is the sample proportion $h = 0.42$. But another sample would have given a slightly different result. How much such results vary can be calculated. For $n = 1000$ the typical deviation is $\sqrt{\tfrac{0.42 \cdot 0.58}{1000}} \approx 0.016$, that is about 1.6 percentage points.

KEY POINT · BASIC TERMS

The population is the set of all objects you want to know something about. A sample is a selection from it, its size is $n$.

A sample is representative if it reflects the population well. Safest is a random selection in which every element has the same chance.

Estimation problem: determine an unknown value (such as a proportion $p$) from the sample. Testing problem: check a conjecture about $p$ with the sample and decide.

The sample proportions spread around $p$ with the standard deviation $\sqrt{\tfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}$.

Bias: if you only ask volunteers or only at one time of day, you do not reach certain groups. A large size does not help against that.

Square root of n: four times as many people asked halve the spread, exactly as with the binomial distribution in Year 12.

INTERACTIVE · MANY SAMPLES FROM ONE POPULATION

Set $p$ and $n$ and draw many samples. Each gives a proportion $h$. Watch how wide the distribution of the $h$ is, and then make $n$ larger.

EXAMPLE 1 · REPRESENTATIVE?

A newspaper wants to know what the town thinks of the new cycle path and lets its readers vote online. 2,400 votes, 70% against. Is that meaningful?

No. Only people who read the newspaper and feel addressed answer, often especially annoyed ones. The sample is not random, despite its size.

EXAMPLE 2 · HOW LARGE MUST n BE?

How large is the typical variation of a sample proportion for $p = 0.5$ with $n = 100$ and $n = 400$?

$\sqrt{\tfrac{0.25}{100}} = 0.05$ and $\sqrt{\tfrac{0.25}{400}} = 0.025$. Four times the size, half the spread.

EXERCISES

Give the population and the sample: a) In a factory 20 screws are measured every hour. b) Before the election 1,200 voters are phoned.

a) all screws produced / the 20 measured   b) all voters / the 1,200 people asked

Estimation or testing problem? a) Is the dice fair? b) How high is the proportion of faulty parts? c) Does the new fertiliser help?

a) test   b) estimation   c) test

In a survey of 1,000 people, 42% name party X. Give a range in which the true proportion lies with great certainty (twice the standard deviation).

$0.42 \pm 2 \cdot 0.016 = [0.389, 0.451]$, that is about 39% to 45%.

How many people do you have to ask so that the standard deviation of the proportion is at most 1 percentage point for $p = 0.5$?

$\sqrt{\tfrac{0.25}{n}} \le 0.01 \Rightarrow n \ge 2500$.

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Sample mean and sample variance

The ten packets weigh exactly 500 g on average. But a machine that fills 480 g and 520 g alternately would have the same mean. How do you measure the spread?

As with random variables in Year 12: via the squared deviations from the mean. For samples you divide by $n - 1$ instead of $n$, because the mean itself was estimated from the data.

KEY POINT · SAMPLE STATISTICS

Sample mean: $\bar{x} = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2 + \ldots + x_n}{n}$

Sample variance: $s^2 = \dfrac{1}{n - 1} \left((x_1 - \bar{x})^2 + \ldots + (x_n - \bar{x})^2\right)$   ·   standard deviation $s = \sqrt{s^2}$

$\bar{x}$ and $s$ estimate the mean $\mu$ and the standard deviation $\sigma$ of the population.

Calculator: many calculators show both values, $s_{n-1}$ (sample) and $\sigma_n$ (dividing by $n$). For samples you take $s_{n-1}$.

EXAMPLE 3 · TEN PACKETS

Calculate $\bar{x}$ and $s$ for 498, 502, 500, 497, 503, 501, 499, 500, 504, 496 g.

$\bar{x} = 500$ g. Deviations $-2, 2, 0, -3, 3, 1, -1, 0, 4, -4$, sum of squares 60. $s^2 = \tfrac{60}{9} \approx 6.67$, $s \approx 2.58$ g.

EXAMPLE 4 · TWO MACHINES

Machine B delivers 480, 520, 490, 510, 500 g. Compare with example 3.

$\bar{x} = 500$ g, sum of squares $400 + 400 + 100 + 100 + 0 = 1000$, $s^2 = 250$, $s \approx 15.8$ g. The same mean, but B spreads six times as much.

EXERCISES

Calculate $\bar{x}$ and $s$ for the measurements 12, 15, 11, 14, 13.

$\bar{x} = 13$, sum of squares $1 + 4 + 4 + 1 + 0 = 10$, $s^2 = 2.5$, $s \approx 1.58$.

In 40 rolls of a dice the mean score was 3.9. Is that unusual for a fair dice? (One roll has $\sigma \approx 1.71$, the mean of 40 rolls $\tfrac{1.71}{\sqrt{40}}$.)

Standard deviation of the mean $\approx 0.27$. $3.9$ is $0.4$ above $3.5$, that is about 1.5 standard deviations: noticeable, but not unusual enough for suspicion.

Why do you divide by $n - 1$ for $s^2$? Think about a sample with only one value.

With $n = 1$, $\bar{x} = x_1$ and every deviation is 0. Dividing by $n$ would give variance 0, as if there were no spread. With $n - 1 = 0$, $s^2$ is not defined at all: from a single value you cannot say anything about the spread. In general $n - 1$ makes up for the fact that $\bar{x}$ lies closer to the data than the true $\mu$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Mean of 12, 15, 11, 14, 13?

13

Sample variance of the values 12, 15, 11, 14, 13?

$\tfrac{10}{4} = 2.5$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A school wants to know how satisfied the students are with the canteen. Describe a good and a bad way to draw the sample.

Good: select at random from the list of students, in all year groups. Bad: only ask those who sit in the canteen at lunchtime; dissatisfied students may eat elsewhere.

Connecting with Year 12: the proportion of left-handed people is about 10%. In a sample of 50 people: how many do you expect, and what is $\sigma$? How likely are 10 or more?

$\mu = 5$, $\sigma = \sqrt{4.5} \approx 2.12$. $P(X \ge 10) \approx 0.025$: rare, but possible.

EXCURSIONSIZE IS NO SUBSTITUTE FOR RANDOM SELECTION

The election of 1936

Before the US presidential election of 1936 the magazine Literary Digest sent out about ten million questionnaires, more than two million came back. Its forecast: the challenger Alf Landon would clearly beat President Franklin D. Roosevelt. In fact Roosevelt won by a large margin.

The addresses came, among other sources, from telephone directories and car registrations, at that time rather well-off people. And it was mainly those who were dissatisfied with the government who answered. The young pollster George Gallup got it right with a much smaller but more carefully selected sample and became famous for it.

Source: Peverill Squire: Why the 1936 Literary Digest Poll Failed. Public Opinion Quarterly 52 (1), 1988.

$\sqrt{\tfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}$, four times $n$ halves it.

$n = 1000$, $p = 0.42$: 1.6 percentage points

STATISTICS

$\bar{x}$ and $s^2 = \tfrac{1}{n-1} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2$

Packets: $\bar{x} = 500$ g, $s \approx 2.58$ g
